entry.title: Dotfiles part 5: per-machine git identity
entry.summary: A shared gitconfig includes ~/.gitconfig.local, so each machine sets its own email and signing key....
entry.content:
Part 5 of my dotfiles series.

The problem#

My personal and work machines commit with different email addresses and different GPG keys. Having a shared gitconfig with hardcoded email and signingkey caused work commits going out under the wrong identity.

The include#

The shared config/git/gitconfig is symlinked to ~/.gitconfig. It sets everything common: delta as the pager, zdiff3 conflicts, main as the default branch, and gpgsign = true. Its last block is:

[include]
path = ~/.gitconfig.local

git reads an included file at the point of the include. Being last, ~/.gitconfig.local overrides anything above it. When the file is missing, git ignores the include without an error.

Where the local file comes from#

Each profile repo holds its own gitconfig.local with email and signingkey. The profile’s install.sh symlinks it to ~/.gitconfig.local. The email and key ID never enter the public repo.

The global gitignore#

The old config set core.excludesfile to an absolute path, /Users/andrew/.dotfiles/.... That broke on any machine with a different username.

With core.excludesfile unset, git reads ~/.config/git/ignore as the global ignore file. So the gitconfig sets nothing, and bin/install symlinks the repo file to that default path:

ln -sfn "$DOTFILES/config/git/gitignore_global" "$HOME/.config/git/ignore"

The path has no username in it, and the gitconfig needs no extra line.

For a while the symlink pointed at ~/.gitignore_global instead. Git never read that file, because nothing in the config named it.

entry.title: Dotfiles part 4: halving zsh startup time
entry.summary: Swapping nvm for fnm and lazy-loading thefuck cut a new shell from about 1.5s to 0.8s....
entry.content:
Part 4 of my dotfiles series.

A new shell took about 1.5 seconds to start. After two changes it now takes about 0.8 seconds. As well as slimming down the oh-my-zsh plugins, these helped a lot too;

nvm to fnm#

nvm (node version manager) is a shell script. Sourcing it on every shell start was the largest single cost. fnm is a compiled Rust binary that does the same job:

command -v fnm &> /dev/null && eval "$(fnm env --use-on-cd)"

--use-on-cd switches Node version when a directory has a .nvmrc or .node-version file for convenient version switching.

Lazy-loading thefuck#

thefuck --alias starts Python to print the alias, about 130ms on every shell start. The alias is rarely needed in a given shell. A small function defers the cost to first use:

if command -v thefuck &> /dev/null; then
  fuck() {
    unfunction fuck
    eval "$(thefuck --alias)"
    fuck "$@"
  }
fi

On the first call, the function deletes itself, defines the real alias, and runs it with the same arguments. Later calls go straight to the alias.

Pointing Starship at its config#

Starship reads ~/.config/starship.toml by default. The symlink lives at ~/.config/starship/starship.toml, so Starship was running without my config. One export fixed it:

export STARSHIP_CONFIG="$HOME/.config/starship/starship.toml"

Next: per-machine git identity.

entry.title: Dotfiles part 3: an idempotent install script
entry.summary: bin/install sets up a new Mac in six steps and does nothing harmful when run again....
entry.content:
Part 3 of my dotfiles series.

When I get a new machine, all I need to do is run two commands:

git clone git@github.com:apepindev/dotfiles.git ~/.dotfiles
~/.dotfiles/bin/install && exec zsh

For me, this doesn’t happen frequently, but when it does come to it, it makes setting it up a breeze.

My old fresh.sh script always assumed it was running on a fresh machine. Naively, it ran rm -rf $HOME/.zshrc, then mkdir $HOME/Code with no -p. A second run stopped at the mkdir. Fixing one step meant running everything again by hand. But now the ~/.dotfiles/bin/install can be run repeatedly after first install because…

Six steps, each one checks first#

  1. oh-my-zsh, installed only when ~/.oh-my-zsh is missing.
  2. Homebrew, installed only when brew is not on PATH.
  3. Symlinks, made with ln -sfn, which replaces an existing link in place.
  4. Machine profile, read from profiles/current or asked for if not set.
  5. Homebrew packages, from config/Brewfile and then the profile’s Brewfile.
  6. The profile’s install.sh hook, when it exists and is executable.

Every step either skips or overwrites. Running the script twice gives the same result as running it once.

Choosing a profile on a fresh machine#

As mentioned on a previous post, profiles are private repos, so a new machine has none. The script lists any profile folders it finds, but it will also accept a new name:

? Which machine profile? [personal work, or a new name]

When that folder is empty, the script asks for a git URL and clones the profile repo into it.

A blank answer scaffolds a new profile instead. The script creates plugins.zsh, aliases.zsh, exports.zsh, paths.zsh, functions.zsh, a Brewfile, a bin/ folder and an executable install.sh. It then runs git init, so the profile only needs a private remote and a push. Existing profile are protected though and never overwritten.

One hook per machine#

The core links nothing machine-specific. Each profile can ship an install.sh, which runs last, after brew bundle, so brew tools are available. $DOTFILES is exported for it. The hook has no rules: symlinks, extra clones, anything.

This replaced a separate clone.sh from my first attempt at managing my dotfiles that was called from fresh.sh.

Output that stays clean in logs#

Colours come from tput, and only when stdout is a terminal:

if [ -t 1 ]; then
  BOLD=$(tput bold); GREEN=$(tput setaf 2)
else
  BOLD=; GREEN=
fi

Piped to a file, the output has no escape codes.

Reloading the shell#

The script used to finish with exec zsh. The script runs as a child process, so that started a new zsh nested under the script. Ghostty then warned that a process was still running when I closed the tab.

Now the script prints exec zsh as the next command. A dotsync function in .functions runs bin/install && exec zsh from the interactive shell, which replaces that shell directly.

Next: halving zsh startup time.

entry.title: Dotfiles part 2: loading machine profiles in zsh
entry.summary: One file names the active profile. The load order matters because oh-my-zsh reads its plugins array once....
entry.content:
Part 2 of my dotfiles series.

Picking the profile#

profiles/current just holds one word, personal or work, or whatever you name the profile directory. bin/install writes it but will ask which existing/new profile to select. It then becomes the first thing .zshrc reads to set the profile for terminal session:

[ -r "$DOTFILES/profiles/current" ] && PROFILE="$(cat "$DOTFILES/profiles/current")"

Plugins come before oh-my-zsh#

oh-my-zsh needs to read the plugins array early and only once when oh-my-zsh.sh is sourced, as a plugin added afterwards never loads. So the profile’s plugins.zsh is sourced and appended to the core plugins early with plugins+=(...). The shared base of git, macos and docker stays in place:

plugins=(git macos docker)
[ -n "$PROFILE" ] && [ -r "$DOTFILES/profiles/$PROFILE/plugins.zsh" ] \
  && source "$DOTFILES/profiles/$PROFILE/plugins.zsh"

source "$ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh"

Shared files, then the profile#

After oh-my-zsh, .zshrc sources the shared .exports, .aliases and .functions. Then it sources every *.zsh in the profile, except plugins.zsh, which is already loaded:

for file in "$DOTFILES_PROFILE_DIR"/*.zsh; do
  [ "$file" = "$DOTFILES_PROFILE_DIR/plugins.zsh" ] && continue
  [ -r "$file" ] && source "$file"
done
prepend_path "$DOTFILES_PROFILE_DIR/bin"

The profile loads after the shared files, so a profile alias takes precedence over a core one with the same name.

Starship starts last with eval "$(starship init zsh)". ZSH_THEME="" just prevents oh-my-zsh drawing its own as I’m just using Starship for the prompt.

Re-sourcing safely#

As source ~/.zshrc runs every line again, a plain PATH="$dir:$PATH" would add a duplicate entry on each reload. prepend_path in .exports adds a directory only when it is missing:

function prepend_path {
  case ":$PATH:" in
    *":$1:"*) :;;
    *) PATH="$1:$PATH";;
  esac
}

Guarded tool setup#

Both machines install the same version managers, but a missing tool shouldn’t break the shell. So each init line checks if the tool exists first:

command -v zoxide &> /dev/null && eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"
command -v rbenv &> /dev/null && eval "$(rbenv init - zsh)"

Aliases for eza (for ls), bat (for cat) and rg (for grep) use the same guard. So for example a machine without eza, ls stays plain ls.

Next: the install script.

entry.title: Dotfiles part 1: a public core with private machine profiles
entry.summary: My dotfiles split into a public repo for shared shell config and one private repo per machine....
entry.content:
This is the first post in a series about my dotfiles and how I manage profiles between separate computers.

  1. A public core with private machine profiles (you are here)
  2. Loading machine profiles in zsh
  3. An idempotent install script
  4. Halving zsh startup time
  5. Per-machine git identity

Where it started#

For a long while I neglected my personal development environments until it got to the point where it was difficult to get full visibility of it. After the millionth time of doing some spring-cleaning I decided to settle on an environment and create a repo for it. It held a .zshrc, a 1,579 line .p10k.zsh for the Powerlevel10k prompt, one Brewfile and a fresh.sh setup script. It was just a dump of what I was using at the time really.

There was a fresh.sh script that ran top to bottom once. It deleted ~/.zshrc, symlinked the repo copy, ran brew bundle and cloned some repos, but this wasn’t something that can run idempotently. That lead to falling into bad habits again and eventually a neglected dotfiles repo very quickly.

Two machines, one repo#

The issue was mainly caused by the fact I’d have separate machines for work and personal use. By early 2026 the repo had a personal.Brewfile and a work.Brewfile side by side. Work aliases and paths sat in the same public files as everything else, which you can imagine was awkward to maintain.

The overhaul#

In July 2026 I came across a post, Freek Van der Herten’s dotfiles and his tour of them, and I was inspired to follow in his footsteps. It’s almost identical really apart from a small, but game changing detail: profiles.

The new layout:

~/.dotfiles/
  bin/install              # bootstrap, safe to re-run
  home/
    .zshrc
    .exports
    .aliases
    .functions
  config/
    Brewfile               # packages for every machine
    ghostty/config
    starship/starship.toml
    zed/settings.json
    git/gitconfig
    git/gitignore_global
    oh-my-zsh/             # shared ZSH_CUSTOM
  profiles/                # contents gitignored
    current                # "personal" or "work"
    personal/              # its own private repo
    work/                  # its own private repo

The split#

The public repo holds config that is true on every machine. Common tool configs across machines, useful aliases and functions, and a single .zshrc. However, Each folder under profiles/ is a separate private git repo that extends from this core environment.

An example profile would look something like this:

profiles/<profile>/
  plugins.zsh    # plugins+=(...)
  aliases.zsh
  exports.zsh
  paths.zsh
  functions.zsh
  Brewfile       # packages beyond config/Brewfile
  bin/           # added to PATH
  install.sh     # optional setup hook

Not all profiles will need to extend (or even override) everything in core. Its purpose is just an extension. For example, I have aliases for K8s that I use for work, but I don’t need or use K8s on my personal machine (not yet anyway), so they’re not in core or my personal profile.

Having this clear separation really helped me get more visibility on my environment.

Symlinks#

It’s a common practice, but bin/install symlinks home/.zshrc to ~/.zshrc and each app config into ~/.config. That way any changes I need to make to my environment is done within the dotfiles repo, which immediately edits the running config. Just needs a shell reload to pick up the change. Simple.

Next: how .zshrc loads the active profile.
